passages.t: One fate for all, and hope among the living
passages.happening:
The Teacher concludes ‘that the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God’s hands’ (verse 1). But no one knows what lies ahead.

‘It is the same for all: There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked, for the good and the bad, for the clean and the unclean, for the one who sacrifices and the one who does not’ (verse 2). ‘This is an evil in everything that is done under the sun: There is one fate for everyone’ (verse 3).

‘There is hope, however, for anyone who is among the living; for even a live dog is better than a dead lion’ (verse 4). ‘For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no further reward, because the memory of them is forgotten’ (verse 5). Their love, hate and envy are gone, and they will never again have a share in what is done under the sun (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 ended with the Teacher unable to comprehend the work of God. Chapter 9 draws out what follows. If no one knows what lies ahead, and death comes to all alike, how should a person live?

Verse 2 is built on pairs of opposites, righteous and wicked, clean and unclean, worshiper and non-worshiper, to show that no distinction matters to death. The word for fate, miqreh, means what happens to a person, and above all death.

Verse 4 is a proverb with a sting. Dogs were despised scavengers, and lions were symbols of royal power. Even so, a live dog is better off than a dead lion, because the living still have hope.

Sheol was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place beneath the earth. The Old Testament rarely speaks of anything beyond it until later texts such as Daniel 12:2 speak of resurrection.
passages.later: Daniel speaks the clearer word that later came: ‘And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt’ (Daniel 12:2). And the Teacher himself will say that ‘the spirit returns to God who gave it’ (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
passages.hard:
Does Ecclesiastes teach that there is no life after death?

Verses 5, 6 and 10 say that the dead know nothing, have no reward, and have no work or knowledge in Sheol. Read alone, they seem to deny any life after death, and some groups have used them to teach that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection.

Several points help. First, the Teacher speaks deliberately of life under the sun, the world as seen from inside human experience, and he says the dead will never again have a share in what is done under the sun (verse 6). He is describing their absence from this world, not giving a full account of their state.

Second, the Old Testament's light on life beyond death is limited and grows over time. Clear words about resurrection come later (Daniel 12:2), and the New Testament grounds its hope in the resurrection of Jesus.

Third, the Teacher himself says elsewhere that the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7), and that God will bring every deed into judgment (12:14), which assumes something beyond the grave.

Christians differ on some details of what happens between death and the resurrection. The church's confession is the resurrection of the body, and this chapter's honesty about death makes that hope all the more weighty. Nothing here says that anyone would be better off dead. The chapter's own word is that the living have hope.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Even a live dog is better than a dead lion, because the living have hope. Ask what hope you are living on today. And ask whom you love, and what you would want to say or do for them while you still have a share in the days under the sun.

passages.happening:
Then comes the book's warmest call to joy. “Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works” (verse 7). ‘Let your garments always be white, and never spare the oil for your head’ (verse 8).

‘Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun’ (verse 9). ‘For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun’ (verse 9).

“Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
White garments were worn at celebrations and suited a hot climate, and oil on the head was a sign of joy and refreshment. These are pictures of a festive life.

The advice closely resembles a passage in an Old Babylonian version of the Gilgamesh Epic, where the alewife Siduri tells the grieving hero that since the gods gave death to humankind, he should fill his belly, make merry, wear clean clothes, cherish the child who holds his hand and let his wife delight in his embrace. The likeness is real, but the setting differs. In Gilgamesh the advice consoles a man who cannot escape death. In Ecclesiastes it rests on the conviction that God has already approved your works and that life is God's gift.

Portion is cheleq, the share God gives. Verse 10 does not counsel despair. Because the time is short, give your whole strength to the work in front of you now.
passages.later: The psalms speak of the same gifts: ‘wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine’ (Psalm 104:15), and ‘You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows’ (Psalm 23:5).
passages.asks: God has already approved your works, so eat your bread with joy. Ask what ordinary gift today you could receive with a glad heart. And ask what work is in front of your hands that deserves all your might.

passages.t: Time and chance, and the poor wise man forgotten
passages.happening:
“I saw something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all” (verse 11). No one knows his time. Like fish caught in a net or birds in a snare, people are caught by an evil time that falls on them suddenly (verse 12).

Then a story. ‘There was a small city with few men. A mighty king came against it, surrounded it, and built large siege ramps against it’ (verse 14). ‘Now a poor wise man was found in the city, and he saved the city by his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man’ (verse 15).

Wisdom is better than strength, the Teacher says, but the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard (verse 16). ‘The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools’ (verse 17). ‘Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Verse 11 does not deny that skill and effort matter. It says they do not guarantee the outcome. Time and chance, what happens to people, come to all.

Siege warfare, with ramps built against a city's walls, was well known in the ancient world. Assyrian palace carvings show such ramps, and one was built at Lachish when Sennacherib besieged it in 701 BC. The story names no king or city, and it may be a parable. Some readers compare it with the wise woman of Abel Beth-maacah, who saved her town from Joab's siege by her counsel (2 Samuel 20:14-22). But the Teacher's story ends differently: no one remembered the man who saved them.

The last verse cuts both ways. Wisdom is stronger than weapons, and one sinner can undo much good.
passages.later: The wise woman of Abel saved her city: ‘Then the woman went to all the people with her wise counsel’ (2 Samuel 20:22). And the Teacher had already said, ‘Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city’ (Ecclesiastes 7:19).
passages.asks: The poor wise man saved a city and was forgotten. Ask whose quiet wisdom you have overlooked because they had no standing. And ask whether you can do good that no one will remember, and do it anyway.
